extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate 18th-century public; writers, actors, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: A short-form periodical essay giving prescriptive and evaluative rules for composing and judging epic poetry (here applied to Milton) alongside miscellany of social and theatrical prescriptions. Primarily literary criticism for educated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of poverty as social strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep one's poverty a secret and govern life by an affectation of closeness and covetousness so as not to feel its weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures illustrated by 'Irus': change dress to appear older and substantial, carry a little oaken cane, keep a steady small stock of ready money, avoid letters and visitors, adopt an air of being a close hunks worth money, use peevishness and reserved manners to repel intimates, let others' expectations of inheritance secure invitations and support, and exploit others' designs to get maintenance (e.g., play at backgammon to cover charges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill in mimicry/acting
rubrics_metrics.description: A mimic or comedian should be able to assume another's air and taciturnity so convincingly that even personal correspondence can be imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close acquaintance with the original subject is necessary; effective mimicry can deceive readers (example: forged letter from Sir Roger). Mimicry combined with natural politeness and sprightly wit makes an actor diverting and socially sought-after.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor's pursuit of critical approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: A player's utmost pride is the approbation of the Spectator (the critic/public opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implications for theatrical entrepreneurs: solicit the critic's favour, tailor service and presentation (e.g., tavern etiquette — 'have no Bells stirring when the Spectator comes'), maintain reputation through quality offerings and courteous servants; approval by influential periodicals or critics is decisive to an actor's or proprietor's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for tavern/wine-trade advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tavern proprietors should advertise and supply 'neat natural wines' from reputable merchants, sold wholesale and retail, promising fidelity and delivery in natural purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendor claims should include the source (best growths), trustworthy agents (e.g., 'trusty Anthony'), assurance of natural purity and faithful service; such assurances are used to win patronage from friends and customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hood colour to complexion and signal use
rubrics_metrics.description: The colour of a lady's hood should be chosen to flatter her complexion and may serve as a signal of humour or political inclination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/opinions: Ovid recommends colours (red-striped silk for pale complexions, white for brown, dark for fair); contemporary rule-of-thumb (Will Honeycomb) — palest features look best in white sarsenet, overflushed faces in deep scarlet, darkest complexions alleviated by black; hood colours are also said to signal moods (flame colour = 'set upon execution', purple = unapproachable, white = peace, black = husband away), and Whig/Tory ladies may even hang out different colours to show principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate mind as well as outward adornment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ladies should excel in virtue and good sense as much as in beauty; cultivate the mind as industriously as the body is adorned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhortation to British ladies: while fashions and ornamentation (e.g., hoods, ribbons) are pursued, equal or greater industry should be devoted to intellectual and moral cultivation; invokes an old Greek aphorism connecting a woman's adornment with wealth and disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: unity — the action should be one
rubrics_metrics.description: The central fable (action) of an epic should be a single action rather than a series of unrelated actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Homer opens in medias res to preserve unity; Virgil likewise limits his principal action to Aeneas's settlement; Milton opens with the Infernal Council and confines other large antecedent events to episodic books to preserve a single principal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: entirety — the action should be complete (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic action must be entire, consisting of a distinct beginning, middle, and end, with no extraneous steps omitted or included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's test of an entire action; examples: the anger of Achilles shown from its birth through its effects; Aeneas's settlement carried through opposition. Milton's action is praised as showing contrivance in Hell, execution on Earth, and punishment in Heaven — growing naturally from part to part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: greatness — importance and due length
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of an epic must be great in consequence (affecting nations or the whole species) and must have a due magnitude or length so that memory can apprehend it satisfactorily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness exemplified: Achilles' anger embroils Greece; Aeneas's settlement births Rome; Milton's subject concerns the Fall of Man (a species-level concern). Aristotle's analogy: action must be neither too short (all seen at once and indiscernible) nor too long (too diffuse for memory). Use episodes and divine machinery to extend a short action agreeably without overcharging memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes — they must arise naturally and not break unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are permissible when they naturally arise from the subject and run parallel with or illuminate the principal action rather than disrupt unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virgil's episodes about Troy are related by way of episode but close to the principal subject; Milton casts antecedent scenes into Books V–VII as episodes that have affinity with his central action. Critics should favor episodes that act as counterparts or copies of the main plot (e.g., the beauty admired in two-plot dramas like The Spanish Fryer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur in principal members and every part
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only the whole poem but its principal members and every part should be great and magnificent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare architecture: parts must match the whole. Milton is praised for an unquestionable magnificence in every part; minor instances in Homer/Virgil (e.g., a book of games or certain similes) may differ in tone but do not detract from the demand that principal portions maintain grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when inventing around sacred or authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When an epic draws on scripture or other sacred/authoritative materials, the poet must proceed with the greatest caution in what is invented and added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton had few traditional circumstances to expand upon and faced the risk of offending religion; yet he managed to add surprising incidents that analogize Scripture closely enough to please delicate readers without giving offense. This is a constraint on permissible invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper moral judgment with compassion (on sexual vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural indulgence or vice ought to place a person beyond the compassion of the virtuous; those who harshly condemn others' sexual failings show questionable sincerity of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: modest women may hate breaches of chastity for themselves but should pity others; public prostitutes often fall through poverty or coercion (e.g., newly come girls taken by bawds), so charity and understanding are due rather than unrelenting scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the economy and instruction of brothels (critique of bawds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bawds operate as businesslike instructors: they catalogue girls, evaluate and 'price' them according to looks, breeding, and social manipulables, and prepare stories to deceive purchasers' relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's (dramatic/observational) account: bawds exam candidates (education, behaviour), set values (e.g., 'maidenhead will amount to some three hundred'), manipulate families (present plate or bribe fathers), and thereby commodify innocence. This functions as a social-critic standard for judging the institutional causes of prostitution and the need for social pity and reform.
